title: Distributed Caches and Locks
summary: Share fast state across services, and coordinate short critical sections safely.
keyPoints: An in-process cache is fast but private to one instance; a shared cache gives the fleet one logical view.
Cache-aside is the default shared-cache pattern, with TTLs, eviction limits, and invalidation on write.
Hot keys, stampedes, and cache outages are capacity events that need sharding, single-flight, and fail-open or fail-closed choices.
A Redis lock needs a unique owner token and an expiry, but a lease can expire while the holder is still running.
Fencing tokens make stale lock holders harmless; the protected resource must reject older tokens.
Use a database transaction or unique constraint for invariants; locks are for short coordination, not long workflows.

complexity.note: No network call, but each instance has its own copy.
One network round trip in the same region.

complexity.time: one lock check plus one storage write
complexity.note: The resource rejects a token below the highest seen.

commonMistakes: Using a distributed lock for a long workflow or an external side effect that can outlive the lease.
Releasing a lock without checking that the caller still owns the same token.
Assuming a lock prevents double booking, then discovering that an expired holder can still write.
Keeping shared counters in per-instance memory so the effective limit multiplies with the fleet.
interviewNotes: Separate local cache, shared cache, and source of truth, and say what stale window each one allows.
Name the eviction policy, TTL, and hot-key or stampede protection for the shared cache.
For a lock, state the lease length, owner token, release check, and fencing token.
Explain why Redlock is not consensus and when ZooKeeper or etcd is a better coordination layer.
Prefer a database transaction, unique constraint, or idempotency key when the invariant lives in one database.

checkYourself.question: Why is a per-instance cache wrong for rate-limit counters?
checkYourself.answer: Each instance counts separately, so the effective limit is multiplied by the number of instances. A shared atomic counter keeps one logical limit.

checkYourself.question: What does a fencing token add to a distributed lock?
checkYourself.answer: It gives each acquisition a monotonically increasing number. The protected resource rejects writes from an older token, so a holder whose lease expired cannot overwrite newer work.

checkYourself.question: When is a unique constraint better than a distributed lock?
checkYourself.answer: When the invariant is in one database and can be enforced by the database. A unique constraint cannot expire or be bypassed by a paused lock holder.
